answers.working: The set is all real t with -9 <= t < 2. The lower end -9 is included (<=) and the upper end 2 is excluded (<). In interval notation that is [-9, 2).
The set is all real x with -2 <= x < 3. The lower end -2 is included (<=) and the upper end 3 is excluded (<). In interval notation that is [-2, 3).
The set is all real x with 6 <= x <= 16. Both ends are included (<=), so the interval is closed: [6, 16].

judge.notes:
Verdict: family REJECTED on the displayed key. The three instances (g001, g005, g008) are typed-answer items with no options, so there are no distractors (distractors_ok true) and no word problem (context_ok true).

KEY FORM (false): the stem asks for interval notation of a set with a stated inclusion pattern. The correct_answer and marker.key text show round brackets on both ends in all three instances, which is wrong for each.
- g001: -9 ≤ t < 2 should be [-9, 2). The key says "(-9, 2)", which is open at -9.
- g005: -2 ≤ x < 3 should be [-2, 3). The key says "(-2, 3)", which is open at -2.
- g008: 6 ≤ x ≤ 16 should be [6, 16]. The key says "(6, 16)", which is open at both ends and so excludes 6 and 16, which are in the set.
The bracket type is the whole point of the question. A student shown "(6, 16)" as the answer learns the exact error the item should teach against.
The answer_check strings do encode the right brackets, assuming the last two arguments are the left-closed and right-closed flags (I could not open the checker to confirm). interval(-9, 2, 1, 0) reads as [-9, 2), and interval(6, 16, 1, 1) as [6, 16]. So the LaTeX/display key and answer_check are not the same expression. A student who types the correct "[-9, 2)" would be marked right but shown a different key.

SOLUTION (false): each worked solution is mathematically correct and ends on the right interval ([-9, 2), [-2, 3), [6, 16]). It does not reach the stated key, because the final step gives a bracketed interval while the key is the all-round-bracket form. The method (smaller number first, ≤ gives a square bracket, < gives a round bracket) is sound. Fixing the key text to match step 4 and answer_check would make this pass.

Fix needed: make correct_answer and marker.key the bracketed LaTeX/text form that matches step 4 and answer_check, i.e. "[-9, 2)", "[-2, 3)" and "[6, 16]". Likely cause: the key renderer or generator drops the bracket type and prints "(lo, hi)" regardless of the closed flags.

answers.working: The set is all real x with x < 4. The inequality is strict, so 4 is excluded and gets a round bracket. The set is unbounded below, so it starts at -∞, which always takes a round bracket. That gives (-∞, 4). Option A puts a square bracket on -∞, which is invalid. Option C is x > 4. Option D includes 4.

The set is all real x with x < -1. The inequality is strict, so -1 is excluded and gets a round bracket. The set extends down to -∞, which takes a round bracket. That gives (-∞, -1). Option A puts a square bracket on -∞, which is invalid. Option B is x > -1. Option C includes -1.

The set is all real x with x ≥ -8. The inequality is non-strict, so -8 is included and gets a square bracket. The set extends up to ∞, which takes a round bracket. That gives [-8, ∞). Option A puts a square bracket on ∞, which is invalid. Option B is x ≤ -8. Option D excludes -8.

judge.notes: I checked all three instances (g006: x<4, g007: x<-1, g010: x≥-8). Keys B, D and C are (-∞,4), (-∞,-1) and [-8,∞), and each is correct and in interval notation, as asked. Every tagged distractor is exactly what a student making that error would write, and each is definitely wrong. The reversed-direction distractor in g010, (-∞,-8], keeps the square bracket that the sign calls for, which is the right behaviour for that error. The worked solutions reach their keys correctly: infinity end, round bracket at infinity, then the bracket at the finite end read from the sign, then the interval. Minor wording point, not wrong: step 4 in every instance says "Write the end on the left first", which is a slightly odd template phrase. answers.working: [1, 4) has a square bracket at 1, so 1 is included (1 ≤ x). It has a round bracket at 4, so 4 is excluded (x < 4). That gives 1 ≤ x < 4, which is option A.
(9, 14) has round brackets at both ends, so both endpoints are excluded. That gives 9 < x < 14, which is option B.
(-3, 2) has round brackets at both ends, so both endpoints are excluded. That gives -3 < x < 2, which is option D.

1<x<4 swaps the sign only at the left end and leaves the right end correct. A consistent bracket/sign swap would not do that. It is a different error (treating the interval as open, or ignoring the square bracket).
1≤x≤4 keeps the left end correct and swaps only the right end. It is a one-endpoint error (treating the interval as closed), not the consistent bracket/sign swap.
9≤x<14 swaps only the left end and leaves the right end correct. A consistent swap on (9,14) gives 9≤x≤14.
9<x≤14 swaps only the right end and leaves the left end correct. This is a partial swap, not what the tagged error produces.
(9,14) with both round brackets read as ≤ gives 9≤x≤14. This is the consistent swap.
-3≤x<2 swaps only the left end. A consistent swap on (-3,2) gives -3≤x≤2.
-3≤x≤2 is the consistent swap, with both round brackets read as ≤.
-3<x≤2 swaps only the right end and leaves the left end correct. This is a partial swap, not the tagged error.

judge.notes:
The keys, solutions and stems are all correct.

Key: g003 is A, which is 1≤x<4, correct for [1,4). g005 is B, which is 9<x<14, correct for (9,14). g008 is D, which is -3<x<2, correct for (-3,2). Every key is in set notation, as the stem asks.

Solutions: each follows the endpoint-by-endpoint method (square bracket means ≤, round bracket means <) and reaches its key correctly.

Context: there is no word problem and the stems are unambiguous.

Every wrong option is definitely wrong. No option is ALSO_CORRECT.

The problem is the misconception tags. All nine wrong options carry mc:...:brackets-swapped-for-signs, but in each instance only one option is what that error produces. That option is the one with every bracket swapped: B in g003, D in g005, B in g008. The other six options flip the sign at one endpoint only. Those are different errors: treating the interval as open, treating it as closed, or reading only one end wrongly.

A student who picks one of those six would be diagnosed with the wrong error, and the tutor would then explain the wrong thing. The same tag on three options also means the options cannot tell the errors apart.

Fix: keep brackets-swapped-for-signs only on the fully swapped option. Give each partial-swap option its own tag, for example one for treating the interval as open at the closed end and one for treating it as closed at the open end. Alternatively, leave those options untagged. In g003 the options with one end flipped (C and D) would need those separate tags.

answers.working: Interval notation describes a continuous run of real numbers with no gaps. N and Z give only isolated whole numbers, and Q skips every irrational between rationals. Only the R option, {x in R, 6<=x<14}, is the interval [6, 14).
Interval notation needs every real number between the endpoints. N, Z and Q all leave gaps, so they are not intervals. Only the R option, {x in R, 7<x<=12}, equals the interval (7, 12].

Interval notation needs every real number between the endpoints. N and Z give a finite list of integers, and Q misses the irrationals. Only the R option, {x in R, 6<=x<=10}, equals the interval [6, 10].

distractors.why: The N set {6,...,13} is a discrete set, not an interval. A student who thinks any 6<=x<14 set can be written as [6,14) regardless of the number system would pick it. Definitely wrong.
The Z set {6,...,13} is discrete, so it cannot be written as an interval. It matches the tagged error and is definitely wrong.

The Q set is dense but is not all of [6,14), because it misses the irrationals. It is the most tempting form of the error and is definitely wrong under the convention that interval notation denotes real intervals.
The N set {8,...,12} is discrete, so it cannot be written as (7,12]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.
The Z set {8,...,12} is discrete, so it cannot be written as (7,12]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.
The Q set omits the irrationals in (7,12], so it is not (7,12]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.
The N set {6,...,10} is discrete, so it cannot be written as [6,10]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.
The Z set {6,...,10} is discrete, so it cannot be written as [6,10]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.
The Q set omits the irrationals in [6,10], so it is not [6,10]. It matches the tagged error and is wrong.

judge.notes:
I checked all three instances (g001, g007, g008) and found no defects.

Key and form: each key is the single R option. The interval stated in the solution matches its inequality: 6<=x<14 gives [6,14), 7<x<=12 gives (7,12], and 6<=x<=10 gives [6,10]. The stem asks only which set can be written in interval notation, so a letter key is the right form.

answers.working: Known points (-6,-15) and (3,12): m = (12-(-15))/(3-(-6)) = 27/9 = 3. Then 12 = 3*3 + c gives c = 3, so y = 3x + 3. Check x=-6: -18+3 = -15 correct. Missing y at x=-3: -9+3 = -6. Missing x at y=3: 3x+3=3 gives x=0.

Known points (-1,-1) and (5,-13): m = (-13-(-1))/(5-(-1)) = -12/6 = -2. Then -1 = -2*(-1) + c gives c = -3, so y = -2x - 3. Missing x at y=-5: -2x-3=-5 gives x=1. Missing y at x=3: -6-3 = -9. Check x=5: -10-3 = -13 correct.

Known points (-1,5) and (5,-19): m = (-19-5)/(5-(-1)) = -24/6 = -4. Then 5 = -4*(-1) + c gives c = 1, so y = -4x + 1. Missing x at y=-3: -4x+1=-3 gives x=1. Missing y at x=3: -12+1 = -11. Check x=5: -20+1 = -19 correct.

judge.notes:
The family has no options (typed expression answer), so there are no distractors to judge.

I checked all three instances independently.
- g002: m = 27/9 = 3 and c = -15 - (-18) = 3, so y = 3x + 3. It gives (-6, -15), (0, 3), (-3, -6) and (3, 12), which matches the completed table (x = 0, y = -6).
- g005: m = -12/6 = -2 and c = -1 - 2 = -3, so y = -2x - 3. It gives x = 1 at y = -5, y = -9 at x = 3 and y = -13 at x = 5, which matches the completed table.
- g007: m = -24/6 = -4 and c = 5 - 4 = 1, so y = -4x + 1. It gives x = 1 at y = -3, y = -11 at x = 3 and y = -19 at x = 5, which matches the completed table.

In every instance the missing x-value is the same whether it comes from the equal x-spacing (step 5) or from solving the found rule for the given y, so the table is unambiguous. Each solution follows the book's method: two complete columns, then slope as the change in y over the change in x, then c by substitution, then the missing cells from the rule. The parenthetical in step 3 about neighbouring columns being 2 or 3 apart is correct in each instance and guards against the real error of taking the per-column change as the slope. The marker key and answer_check are the same expression in all three (for example "y = (-2)x - 3" and "y = -2*x - 3").

One cosmetic point, not an error: the stored correct_answer for g005 and g007 reads "y = (-2)x - 3" and "y = (-4)x + 1", with parentheses around a negative slope. The worked solution's last step writes "y = -2x - 3" and "y = -4x + 1". The two are equivalent, but if correct_answer is shown to the student, a template change to "y = -2x - 3" would be tidier. Substitute each x into y = -4x + 5: x=-2 gives 8+5=13; x=-1 gives 4+5=9; x=0 gives 5; x=1 gives -4+5=1; x=2 gives -8+5=-3.

judge.notes:
Verdict: reject on key form only. The maths, context and worked solutions are all fine.

No options: all three instances (g002, g004, g005) are typed-answer (expression, marker kind "interval"), so distractors_ok is vacuously true.

key_form_ok is false for two reasons.
1. The stem asks for the range "as an inequality in h". The worked solution ends with an inequality ($300 \le h \le 600$), but the stored correct_answer / marker key is "(300, 600)", which is not an inequality. It is interval notation.
2. In standard notation round brackets mean open endpoints, so "(300, 600)" excludes 300 and 600. The range is closed, because the graph reaches both extremes, and the solution itself says $\le$. The answer_check "interval(300, 600, 1, 1)" presumably carries the closed-endpoint flags, but the displayed key does not. Anywhere "(300, 600)" is shown as the model answer, it teaches an open interval, which is wrong. Wherever the key is compared with the student's input, it also fails to say that a typed "300 <= h <= 600" is the expected form. I was restricted to the one packet file, so I could not confirm how the interval() checker handles the inequality syntax or the flags. The key should be shown as `300 \le h \le 600` or `[300, 600]`, with answer_check and key matching, and the checker should be confirmed to accept the inequality form the stem asks for.

Maths, which I checked for each instance:
- g002: points (0,350), (2,300), (5,600), (6,450). Min 300 at t=2, max 600 at t=5. Start 350 and finish 450 are both strictly inside, so step 4 is true. Key 300 to 600.
- g004: points (0,250), (1,150), (3,500), (5,350). Min 150 at t=1, max 500 at t=3. Start 250 and finish 350 are inside. Key 150 to 500.
- g005: points (0,300), (2,200), (5,500), (6,350). Min 200 at t=2, max 500 at t=5. Start 300 and finish 350 are inside. Key 200 to 500.

solution_ok is true. Each solution reads the range off the vertical extremes at the right times, rules out the "start to finish" shortcut correctly, and ends with the closed inequality. Step 2's phrase "never goes higher or lower than one of these points" is slightly loose, but it is not wrong, because straight segments take their extremes at the vertices.

context_ok is true. The hiker context is kept, and heights of 150 to 600 m and times of 0 to 6 h are realistic. The graph is fully determined by the four listed points, so nothing needs a picture, and the stem is unambiguous. "Leaving out the units" is clear.

answers.working: Line from (0,0) to (180,120) has slope 120/180 = 2/3 km per minute. 2 hours = 120 min, so distance travelled = 120 x 2/3 = 80 km. Total journey is 120 km, so remaining = 120 - 80 = 40 km.
Line from (0,0) to (150,90) has slope 90/150 = 0.6 km per minute. 2 hours = 120 min, so distance travelled = 0.6 x 120 = 72 km. Total journey is 90 km, so remaining = 90 - 72 = 18 km.
Line from (0,0) to (150,100) has slope 100/150 = 2/3 km per minute. 1 hour = 60 min, so distance travelled = 60 x 2/3 = 40 km. Total journey is 100 km, so remaining = 100 - 40 = 60 km.

judge.notes: The family has no options, so there are no distractors to judge. I recomputed all three instances. g001: s(120) = (120/180) x 120 = 80, and 120 - 80 = 40. g006: s(120) = (90/150) x 120 = 72, and 90 - 72 = 18. g007: s(60) = (100/150) x 60 = 40, and 100 - 40 = 60. Each key matches the stem, which asks for the kilometres still to travel, so the answer is whole journey minus distance already travelled, not the distance covered. Each key is a bare number and the stem fixes the unit as km. The worked solutions follow the same order each time. Step 1 reads the end of the journey from the closed dot. Step 2 converts hours to minutes and checks the time is in the domain: 120 <= 180, 120 <= 150 and 60 <= 150 all hold. Step 3 uses proportionality on a line through the origin. Step 4 subtracts. The implied speeds are realistic: 40, 36 and 40 km/h. The stem is self-contained, because the graph is fully described in text. The hours-to-minutes conversion is the intended difficulty for the advanced tier. In g001 the time 120 min equals the maximum distance 120 km, which is a coincidence and does not make the question ambiguous. The only soft point is that the book's method is probably reading a drawn graph, and here the line is described, so proportion is the natural route. I do not count that as an error.

answers.working: s(t) is the distance still to roll. The line goes from (0,6) to (12,0), so slope = -6/12 = -1/2 and s(t) = 6 - t/2. Rolled 4 m means s = 6 - 4 = 2. Solve 6 - t/2 = 2, so t/2 = 4 and t = 8.
The line goes from (0,15) to (45,0), so slope = -15/45 = -1/3 and s(t) = 15 - t/3. Rolled 5 m means s = 15 - 5 = 10. Solve 15 - t/3 = 10, so t/3 = 5 and t = 15.
The line goes from (0,12) to (36,0), so slope = -12/36 = -1/3 and s(t) = 12 - t/3. Rolled 9 m means s = 12 - 9 = 3. Solve 12 - t/3 = 3, so t/3 = 9 and t = 27.

judge.notes:
The family is numeric with no options, so there are no distractors to judge. I recomputed all three instances from s(t) = L - (L/T)t.

- g004: L=6, T=12, so s = 6 - t/2. Rolled 4 m leaves 2 m, giving t = 8. The key "8" is correct, and the check point (8, 2) lies on the line.
- g007: L=15, T=45, so s = 15 - t/3. Rolled 5 m leaves 10 m, giving t = 15. The key "15" is correct, and (15, 10) is on the line.
- g008: L=12, T=36, so s = 12 - t/3. Rolled 9 m leaves 3 m, giving t = 27. The key "27" is correct, and (27, 3) is on the line.

Key form: the stem asks "after how many seconds", and each key is the bare number of seconds, which is the asked form.

Context: the stem states that the graph shows the distance still to roll, and the question asks about distance already rolled. That is a deliberate trap, and the wording is unambiguous. The line's endpoints are stated in text, so no missing figure is needed. The speeds are slow for a ball (0.33 to 0.5 m/s) but realistic enough for a constant-speed straight-line graph, and the numbers are clean integers.

Solutions: each follows the same three steps. Step 1 converts rolled to remaining distance. Step 2 gives the rate from the endpoints (seconds per metre). Step 3 multiplies and checks that the point is on the line. The arithmetic is correct in all three, and nothing in them teaches a wrong idea.

answers.working: -6x + 5y = 30. Set y=0: -6x = 30, so x = -5. Set x=0: 5y = 30, so y = 6. Rewrite as y = (6/5)x + 6, so the gradient 6/5 is positive and the graph is increasing. This matches x-int -5, y-int 6, increasing.
3x + 6y = 6. Set y=0: 3x = 6, so x = 2. Set x=0: 6y = 6, so y = 1. Rewrite as y = -(1/2)x + 1, so the gradient -1/2 is negative and the graph is decreasing. This matches x-int 2, y-int 1, decreasing.

2x + 6y = 12. Set y=0: 2x = 12, so x = 6. Set x=0: 6y = 12, so y = 2. Rewrite as y = -(1/3)x + 2, so the gradient -1/3 is negative and the graph is decreasing. This matches x-int 6, y-int 2, decreasing.

y = -x^2 - 4 has the form y = a*x^2 + c with no x term, so the axis of symmetry is x = 0. At x = 0, y = -4. Since a = -1 < 0 the parabola opens down, so this is a maximum turning point.

judge.notes:
The family is a typed-answer family (answer type expression, marker kind coordinates) and none of the three instances has options, so there are no distractors to judge.

answers.working: First and third quadrants means a > 0. Further from the axes than y = 6/x means a > 6. Shifting 5 units up gives y = a/x + 5. So we need a > 6 and a +5 constant. A: a = 5 (not > 6), B: a negative, C: shifted down by 5. D: a = 9 > 6 and +5, which fits.

Second and fourth quadrants means a < 0. Further from the axes than y = 4/x means |a| > 4. Shifting 4 units up gives y = a/x + 4. A: |a| = 1 (not > 4). B: shifted down 4. C: a positive. D: a = -6 (|a| = 6 > 4) and +4, which fits.

Second and fourth quadrants means a < 0. Closer to the axes than y = 6/x means |a| < 6. Shifting 6 units up gives y = a/x + 6. A: shifted down 6. B: a positive. C: |a| = 8 (not < 6). D: a = -4 (|a| = 4 < 6) and +6, which fits.

Right sign and shift, but |a|=8 is greater than 6, so it lies further from the axes, not closer. A student who thinks a bigger a is closer to the axes picks a larger |a| for 'closer'. Definitely wrong.

judge.notes: I found no defects in any of the three instances. I checked each against the book's y=a/x+q rules: the sign of a sets the quadrants, a larger |a| lies further from the axes, and q>0 shifts the graph up. In every instance exactly one option (D) satisfies all three conditions: quadrant pair, |a| relative to the reference, and shift direction. Each of the other three options breaks exactly one condition. Each tagged distractor matches its misconception: smaller |a| when the student wants 'further' (or larger |a| for 'closer'), the correct size with the opposite sign, and the correct a with q negated. The stems say 'before it is shifted', so the quadrant clue is not confused with the shifted graph. 'Could be' is safe because only D qualifies. The worked solutions run correctly through sign, then size, then q, then selection, and all agree with the keys. Step 4's 'positive value of a with |a|=9' is slightly redundant but not wrong. One non-blocking observation: all three instances have key D, so the options need shuffling or randomising at serve time, otherwise a student can learn that D is always right. The correct answer is also always the one whose numbers never change between options, but that is a generator-wide pattern rather than an error here.

judge.notes:
I checked all three instances (g005, g007, g010) and found no defects.

Key and solution: the book's rule is that a larger |a| puts the hyperbola further from the axes, and the sign of a only sets the quadrants. The correct answers follow from the smallest |a|: g005 gives D, y=-1/(4x), from |a| of 1/4, 1/3, 8, 9; g007 gives A, y=-1/(4x), from 1/4, 3, 7, 8; g010 gives D, y=2/x, from 2, 3, 4, 5. Each key letter matches its choice text. The worked steps list the sizes correctly, pick the smallest, and carry the right closing note about negative a.

Distractors: each tagged wrong option is exactly what the named error produces.
- bigger-a-closer-to-axes picks the largest a, which is also the largest |a|, so there is no ambiguity.
- negative-a-taken-as-small picks the most negative a, namely -8, -3 and -4 in the three instances. Each of these is wrong because its |a| is large.
- The untagged options (1/3, 7/x, -3/x) all have a larger |a| than the key, so they are wrong.

Minor points, not enough to reject:
- The stem says the hyperbolas "are drawn" but gives no figure, so the equations in the options carry the question. It is still unambiguous and answerable.
- y=1/(3x) and y=-1/(4x) are a/x with a fractional a. They are equivalent to the stated form, and a Grade 10 student will read them that way.
- In g005 and g007 the key itself is negative, so a student with the negative-a error may land on the right letter by chance. The error's own pick (-8 or -3) still sits among the options, so the item works.
- In g010 the untagged C (-3/x) could also attract a student with the negative-a error, but it is wrong, which is all it needs.

judge.notes: All three instances check out. Maths: for y=a/x, a>0 puts the graph in quadrants 1 and 3, and a larger |a| puts it further from the axes. The keys are g003 C (7/x, bigger than 5), g005 C (1/x, smaller than 6) and g006 B (5/x, smaller than 6). Each has exactly one option that is both positive and on the correct side of the comparison, so there is no ALSO_CORRECT risk. Every tagged distractor is the product of its stated error: bigger-a-closer-to-axes gives a positive a on the wrong side of k, and sign-of-a-ignored gives the right size with a negative sign. Each family has the three-way split correct, wrong-size positive, and wrong-sign (one right size, one wrong size). The key form fits "which could be the equation", and the stem is unambiguous at Grade 10 level, since comparing the two curves pointwise is well defined. Worked solutions follow the book's method in three steps (sign, size, select). Their statements are true, and step 3 correctly covers all the rejected options. Minor, non-blocking: g005 and g006 have identical stems (same k=6, same direction) and differ only in options and key, so they are near-duplicate items for a student who sees both. answers.working: f(x) = 5/x - 2 and g(x) = 5/x + 3 have the same 5/x part, so only the constant differs. g - f = 3 - (-2) = +5, so the graph moves up 5 units. That is option B.

distractors.why: Treats the change in q as a horizontal move (increase read as right). Magnitude 5 is the change in q. Wrong for the hyperbola, since g has the same asymptote x=0 as f.
Right size (5) but reversed direction: q goes from -2 to 3, so the graph moves up, not down. Matches shift-direction-reversed.
Reads the shift from g's q alone (q=3, up 3) instead of the change from -2 to 3. Matches shift-from-q-alone, and 3 up is wrong.
Treats the change in q as a horizontal move (decrease read as left), magnitude 8. Consistent with the g001 direction mapping. Definitely wrong, since the asymptote stays x=0.
Uses g's q = -2 alone, so 2 units down, rather than the change from 6 to -2, which is 8. Matches shift-from-q-alone, and is wrong.
Right size (8) but up instead of down. Matches shift-direction-reversed, and is wrong.
Right size (5) but up instead of down, since q goes from -1 to -6. Matches shift-direction-reversed, and is wrong.
Treats the decrease in q as a left shift of 5. Matches q-shifts-sideways and the direction mapping used in g001 and g003, and is wrong.
Uses g's q = -6 alone, so 6 units down, instead of the change from -1 to -6, which is 5. Matches shift-from-q-alone, and is wrong.

judge.notes: Checked all three instances arithmetically. g001: q goes from -2 to 3, up 5 (key B). g003: q goes from 6 to -2, down 8 (key D). g007: q goes from -1 to -6, down 5 (key C). Each key is the only correct option. The tagged distractors each match their misconception. Sideways: the change in q is used as a horizontal move, increase to right and decrease to left. Reversed: right size, wrong direction. From-q-alone: g's new q is used as the shift, such as 3 up, 2 down and 6 down. The sideways direction mapping is consistent across the family. A student with that error could equally pick the opposite direction (the x+p convention), but the option is still a genuine, definitely-wrong distractor, so I did not fail it. No two options in any instance coincide in value, and none is accidentally correct. The solutions reach each key by the book's method (same a, compare q, a rise in q is up and a fall is down), and the step 2 arithmetic is right. Minor nit, not a defect: the stem never names a and q, while the solution uses them. These are the book's notation for y = a/x + q, so I treated it as acceptable. The context is plain and unambiguous, and f is moved to g, which matches the 'f is shifted' wording of the options.

answers.working: y = -9/x + 5. x-intercept: set y = 0, so 9/x = 5, giving x = 9/5. x cannot be 0 (division by zero). The horizontal asymptote is y = 5, so y never equals 5.
y = -1/x + 5. x-intercept: set y = 0, so 1/x = 5, giving x = 1/5. x cannot be 0. The horizontal asymptote is y = 5, so y never equals 5.
y = -7/x - 3. x-intercept: set y = 0, so -7/x = 3, giving x = -7/3. x cannot be 0. The horizontal asymptote is y = -3, so y never equals -3.

judge.notes:
The family has no multiple-choice options, so there are no distractors to judge. I re-derived all three instances independently and every key is correct.

- g004, y=-9/x+5: setting y=0 gives 9/x=5, so x=9/5. The domain excludes 0 and the range excludes 5. Key "9/5, 0, 5" matches answer_check [9/5, 0, 5].
- g007, y=-1/x+5: x=1/5, domain excludes 0, range excludes 5. Key matches.
- g009, y=-7/x-3: x=-7/3. Substituting back gives y=3-3=0, so it checks. The domain excludes 0 and the range excludes -3. Key "-7/3, 0, -3" matches answer_check [-7/3, 0, -3].

Key form: the stem asks for (a), (b), (c) in order, comma-separated, with (a) a fraction in lowest terms. The key gives exactly that. The marker kind is "values" and the LaTeX key is the same list as answer_check in all three.

Context: there is no word problem. The stem is the book's hyperbola y=a/x+q with domain x≠0 and range y≠q, and its (a), (b), (c) wording is unambiguous.

Solutions: all three follow the book's method. They set y=0, multiply by x, isolate the x term, divide, then state the domain from the denominator and the range from the fraction never equalling 0. Each step is arithmetically correct, including the sign handling in g009 (-3x=7, x=7/(-3)=-7/3).

One cosmetic defect, not an error. Step 4 of g004 reads "x=\frac{9}{5}=\frac{9}{5}" and g007 reads "x=\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{5}". That is a template artifact where the "simplify" slot repeats the same fraction. It is harmless but looks odd to a student, so the template should omit the repeated "=" term when the fraction is already in lowest terms. I did not mark solution_ok false because the working is correct and teaches no wrong idea.

answers.working: The y-intercept needs x = 0. In y = 6/x - 1, x = 0 makes 6/x undefined. The graph is a hyperbola with the y-axis (x = 0) as its vertical asymptote, so it never touches the y-axis. The -1 only shifts the horizontal asymptote to y = -1, which is not a y-intercept. Option D, (0, -1), is wrong because the curve never reaches that point.

Set x = 0 in y = -1/x + 6. The term -1/x is undefined at x = 0, so there is no point on the graph with x = 0. The graph is a reflected hyperbola with vertical asymptote x = 0 (the y-axis), so it never crosses the y-axis. The +6 only sets the horizontal asymptote y = 6, so (0, 6) is not on the graph.

Set x = 0 in y = -3/x - 2. The term -3/x is undefined at x = 0, so no point on the graph has x = 0. The vertical asymptote is the y-axis itself, so the curve never meets it. The -2 only sets the horizontal asymptote y = -2, so (0, -2) is not on the graph.

distractors.why: (0,0) is the student who assumes the hyperbola passes through the origin. Definitely wrong, since x=0 makes 6/x undefined.
Setting y=0 in y=6/x-1 gives x=6, which is the x-intercept. Reporting that value as the y-coordinate gives (0,6), so this is the swapped-roles error. Wrong, because no y-intercept exists.
(0,-1) drops the 6/x term and keeps the constant q, which is the assumes-a-y-intercept-exists error. Wrong, because 6/0 is undefined.
